title: Priscilla and Aquila (Acts 18)
hookLine: a tentmaking couple teach eloquent Apollos more accurately, aside from the crowd
tomorrow: why would new believers set fire to their own books?

lines: A TYPO ON THE BIG SCREEN.
cards: A typo on the big screen, mid-presentation. Do you call it out, or catch the speaker after? Acts has an answer.
In Corinth, Paul meets a couple, Aquila and his wife Priscilla, and "by their occupation they were tentmakers," his own trade, so he stays and works beside them.
Later, in Ephesus, a gifted preacher named Apollos gets something partly wrong, in public. The ones who set him right are that tentmaking couple, and they do it away from the crowd.

teach.b: Today's question: how do you tell someone they've got it wrong without crushing them? Here's how Acts tells it. Apollos is "a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures."
He's getting a great deal right. One piece is missing: he knows "only the baptism of John." Priscilla and Aquila hear him in the synagogue, and they don't stand up and fix him in front of the room.
"They took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly." Took him unto them: aside. More perfectly: not starting him over, adding what was missing.
Apollos takes it, and goes on to help many believers. Now a neighbor. Judaism has a commandment for this exact moment.
Leviticus, in the Jewish Publication Society's translation: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart; thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbour."
Jewish teachers call it tochachah, loving correction, and the Talmud reads the end of that verse as a limit: correct him, but not in a way that shames him.
That's the one to tell a friend tonight: both traditions say speak up rather than stew, and guard the other person's face while you do it.

The honest difference: in Judaism this is a mitzvah, a commandment, with rabbis weighing how and when; Acts gives no rule here, only a story, and what the couple adds is teaching about Jesus, which Jews and Christians hold differently.

how: Christians remember Priscilla and Aquila when they read Acts 18 and Paul's letters, and some churches keep a day for the couple.

o: a married pair who argued with Paul in court
a tentmaking couple who taught a preacher kindly
two apostles who wrote letters to Corinth

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: eloquent and mighty in the scriptures
rebuke, rather than hate in your heart

s: more perfectly means Apollos had it all wrong before
he was already mighty in the scriptures. they added what was missing.
Priscilla and Aquila corrected Apollos in front of everyone
they took him unto them: aside, into their own company.
the Torah commands correcting your neighbor instead of hating him
Leviticus 19:17, which Jewish teachers call tochachah.

games.q: a teammate keeps showing the new kids a drill the coach changed last week. she's good, and she means well. what would Priscilla and Aquila do?
o: catch her after practice and kindly fill in the change.
correct her right then, so the new kids hear it too.
say nothing; she's good, and she'll figure it out.
games.why: they took him unto them and expounded the way more perfectly: aside, kindly, adding to what was already good.

practice: Close your eyes and recall a time someone set you right kindly, out of everyone's view. Stay with what made it easy to hear: their tone, their timing, the fact that nobody else was watching.
If you pray, you can ask for a kind tongue.

wordCard.voice: Priscilla and Aquila. Two tentmakers who took a gifted preacher aside and showed him the way of God more perfectly.

orig.note: Greek: more exactly, the word the King James gives as more perfectly in Acts 18:26.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: more perfectly, which means adding what's missing, not starting over. Day done.
